Emphasizes CFIA commercial vs personal rules and CDC Dog Import Form. Critical compliance warnings Canada (CFIA): Determine the import category from ownership, the importer and intended use, not the escort’s volunteer status alone. CFIA has personal pathways for accompanied and unaccompanied pets; dogs intended for adoption, fostering or transfer are commercial imports. Confirm the applicable conditions before booking. Canada prohibits commercial dog imports from countries on CFIA’s high-risk dog-rabies list until further notice; import permits are not issued for those imports. Check CFIA’s list, not the CDC list, before committing to transport. Confirm on official CFIA guidance before the flight. Volunteers: Volunteering is not an import category or a blanket exemption. In the US, APHIS Animal Care regulates resale, including fee-based adoption after import, but lists dogs adopted abroad and delivered to their owners without further resale as outside that AWA scope. CDC, other APHIS and state requirements still apply. Canada uses its own commercial-import definitions. USA (CDC): Almost every dog needs a CDC Dog Import Form receipt. High-risk vs low-risk pathways differ. Mexico (SENASICA): For pet dogs travelling from the US to Mexico, follow OISA/SENASICA entry inspection and the NWS inspection-document requirement effective August 3, 2026. Dogs entering the US from Mexico require separate screwworm-freedom certification. Confirm export requirements for the actual origin and purpose of movement. pages.b: Pet insurance for travelers (US): what policies cover away from home If your dog or cat gets sick or hurt on a trip, will your US pet insurance pay? It depends on where you are, how long you’ve had the policy and what it excludes. Below: what to check, and what 11 US insurers say on their own websites about travel coverage, waiting periods, age limits and reimbursement. Disclosure: every link on this page goes to the insurer’s own official site. We have no affiliate relationship with any insurer. Not advice: PetPolicyCheck is not a licensed insurance agent or broker and does not sell, solicit or negotiate insurance. We provide general information only, not insurance advice. Coverage, availability and prices vary by state and are set by the insurer. Always read the policy documents and confirm details with the insurer. Quick answer US and Canada: most policies we checked reimburse care at any licensed vet in the US, and most also in Canada (some only during a temporary stay). Lemonade covers the US only. Outside the US and Canada: only Embrace and Nationwide say their policies cover vet care abroad. The rest limit cover to the US (and usually Canada), sometimes adding US territories or military bases, or their sites don’t say (marked “Check” in the table). Waiting periods: illness cover usually starts only after a waiting period of up to 30 days (14 or 15 days at most insurers we checked), so a policy bought the week before a trip may not cover that trip. Pre-existing conditions are generally not covered, and that includes anything that first shows up during a waiting period. You pay first: pet insurance usually reimburses you after you pay the vet, so budget for the full bill on the road. Policies differ by state, product and underwriting company, and insurers change
